lessonRef.subject: financial-literacy
lessonRef.unitTitle: PF6 — Protecting and Insuring: Naming Risk and Deciding What to Do About It
lessonRef.title: Applied simulation: identity protection and everyday safeguards

objective: Price the cost of recovering from a fictional identity theft, compare it with the cost of two safeguards, and decide which safeguard is worth its price.
scenario: A fictional person’s details appear in a simulated data breach. The cleanup costs and the safeguard prices below are invented for this exercise. Nothing here asks for or refers to any real personal information.
safetyNotes: Every figure, person, employer, institution, offer, account, and document on this task sheet is fictional and exists only for practice.
No real transaction is part of this lesson, and no real bank, card, brokerage, tax, or login detail is ever requested. If a task sheet ever appears to ask for one, stop and tell a trusted adult.
This lesson teaches general financial concepts and does not advise anyone about their own money. For a real decision, talk with a trusted adult or a qualified licensed professional.
materials: the fictional cleanup and safeguard figures in these directions

tasks.directions: The fictional cleanup takes 26 hours of the person’s own time, of which 6 hours are taken from paid work at $17.20 an hour. Fees for certified post and replacement documents come to $145. The chance of a breach leading to this kind of cleanup in a year is 4%.

prompts.text: What are the lost wages from the 6 hours taken from paid work?
What is the total out-of-pocket and lost-wage cost of one cleanup?
What is the expected annual cost of this risk at a 4% chance?

tasks.directions: Two safeguards are available. A credit freeze costs nothing and blocks most new accounts from being opened in the person’s name; it does not stop misuse of accounts that already exist. A monitoring service costs $14.99 a month and alerts the person after something has already happened.

prompts.text: What does the monitoring service cost for a year?
Compared with the expected annual cost of the risk, is the monitoring service worth its price on these figures alone?
choices: Yes, it costs less than the expected loss
No, it costs more than the expected loss

prompts.text: How much more does the monitoring service cost than the expected annual loss?

The free safeguard prevents the loss and the paid one reports it afterwards. Explain why that difference matters more than the price, and name two figures in this lesson that a real decision would need but that the calculation above does not contain.

remediation: If all 26 hours are being priced at $17.20, reread the directions: only 6 of them were taken from paid work. The other 20 are a real cost with no dollar figure attached, which is worth naming rather than inventing a number for.
extension: Price all 26 hours at the $17.20 wage, recompute the comparison, and say whether that changes the conclusion about the monitoring service.
